reason: Refuted, and not on the French. The French is sound: no quarrel with page 280 of Correspondance tome IV, the letter headed A Madame Tennant, Jour de Noel 1876, reading soyez regle dans votre vie et ordinaire comme un bourgeois, afin d etre violent et original dans vos oeuvres. The English is the problem, on two counts that compound. First, rule 4 of the month is not optional: a translated line names the translator and the year of the published translation whose wording it uses, and the citation standard is that a line ships only in wording that exists in a named edition or a named published translation. The proposal answers translator unidentified. An English sentence that no named translation is known to print is not a hedge about a locator; it is wording with no edition behind it, which is what minting means. The hedge clause covers a trail that runs out on attribution or place. It cannot waive the one rule that exists to stop translation drift, which the brief itself calls this track's main failure mode. Second, the anonymity is not harmless, because the wording is not a faithful rendering. Flaubert wrote ordinaire, ordinary, and the circulating English turns it into orderly and then hangs like a bourgeois on the whole clause, so the sentence loses the point it is famous for, that the artist should be ordinary as a bourgeois. The long investigation of exactly this line at drmlgodin.com reaches the same conclusion, names no translator, and singles out orderly for ordinaire as the substantive error; Wikiquote prints the same English beside the French and the archive.org page 280 link with no translator at all. I tried to rescue it and could not. Internet Archive metadata and advanced search return nothing for the phrase, every search-inside and fulltext endpoint on the Flaubert letters volumes is closed because they are lending only, HathiTrust sits behind a challenge page, and the Google Books API is out of quota, so the Steegmuller claim stays untested in both directions. Two named candidates are worth opening before this line is proposed again: Steegmuller's one-volume Selected Letters of Gustave Flaubert (Farrar, Straus and Young, 1953) and his Letters of Gustave Flaubert 1857 to 1880 (Harvard, 1982), the volume that would cover an 1876 letter. If either prints the sentence, cite that volume and its wording, whatever the wording turns out to be; if neither does, the line is not shippable in English. Two smaller faults while it is down: the source line orders author, locator, work, page rather than author, work, locator, translation as rule 5 requires, and the parenthesis carries a disclaimer where the rule wants the translation. Everything else is clean, so this is purely a citation refutation: shipped.js gives no exact match, no near match, Flaubert at one of three (month 6), not banned; 121 characters; Correspondence is the form. Fit is also thin for a month of stillness and silence, since the line is about discipline and routine rather than quiet, but that is a curator's judgement and not the ground.
